lines.text: Lesson thirteen: liquidation, funding and futures risks. What can close a position for you.
Imagine you open a 10x long. Then BTC falls, and you see this.
Your position was closed by the exchange. You didn't press anything.
That's called liquidation. Let's see how it happens, step by step.
Start with your margin balance: your margin plus the open profit or loss.
A 10x long: 100 USDT of margin, 1,000 USDT notional, entry 60,000.
BTC falls 1%: 90 left. Falls 3%: 70 left. Falls 5%: only 50 left.
Each fall eats into the room left above the maintenance level.
Liquidation is a forced closure. The exchange closes your position for you.
It happens when your margin balance falls to the maintenance level.
You don't choose the price or the moment. Most or all of the margin can be gone.
Like a rental firm taking the car back early. Each exchange has its own rules.
Leverage changes how much room you have.
Same 1,000 USDT position. At 10x you put in 100. At 4x, 250.
A 5% fall costs 50 USDT either way. At 10x, half your margin is gone. At 4x, a fifth.
More room is not safety. A big enough move can reach any level.
Exchanges usually check liquidation against the mark price, not only the last trade.
The mark price is a reference price the exchange works out, often from several markets.
Here one odd trade spikes down. The last price jumps. The mark price moves much less.
But in a real crash, it falls too.
Now funding. Perpetual futures never expire, so they need a way to stay near the spot price.
The funding rate sets a payment between longs and shorts, at set times, often every 8 hours.
Positive rate: longs pay shorts. Negative rate: shorts pay longs.
Example: 1,000 USDT times 0.01% is 0.10 USDT each time.
Funding adds up when you hold a position for a long time.
Three times a day for three days is nine payments: 0.90 USDT at 1,000 notional.
At 10,000 notional, 9 USDT. Real rates change, and can be much higher.
Funding comes out of your margin balance too.
Gap risk. Sometimes price jumps from one level to another, with no trades in between.
Your stop-loss is at 59,000. News hits. Price jumps from 59,600 straight to 58,300.
The stop triggers, but it fills near 58,300. A bigger loss than planned.
A gap can bring liquidation just as suddenly.
A common mistake: thinking a stop-loss protects you from liquidation.
With high leverage, the liquidation zone can sit closer than your stop.
Then the position is liquidated before the stop is ever reached.
And in a gap, a stop can fill late. A stop-loss is not liquidation insurance.
Your turn. BTC is swinging hard before big news. Your buffer is small. You're unsure.
What's the sensible choice: A, B or C? Pause if you need more time.
C. Reduce your exposure or close, then wait. No trade is a real decision.
Adding leverage to win it back makes the next move hit harder.
Before you go further, know the risks of futures.
Liquidation can take most or all of your margin, at a price you didn't choose.
Funding is paid or charged every period, and the rate keeps changing.
Gaps and slippage can make exits worse than planned.
No strategy is guaranteed safe. When unsure, reduce exposure or choose no trade.
Let's recap.
Liquidation is a forced closure when your margin balance hits the maintenance level.
Funding is a regular payment between longs and shorts on perpetual futures.
A stop-loss is not liquidation insurance. Waiting is always allowed.
Check yourself: can a stop-loss guarantee you won't be liquidated?
No. Stops can slip, and liquidation can come first.
Phase 3 complete! Next up: Checkpoint A, a review of lessons T01 to T13.
